content: Humanitarian contexts can significantly hinder the implementation of parenting interventions. While families residing in camp settings, where humanitarian staff provide parenting services, may have relatively easy access to these interventions, it is often challenging to reach families who are dispersed or living in areas affected by armed conflict. Furthermore, formal systems for health, social welfare, and other essential services are frequently degraded or destroyed in such settings, necessitating the use of alternative mechanisms for delivering interventions. To ensure that parenting interventions in these circumstances are effectively integrated into broader humanitarian efforts, their selection, delivery, and monitoring should align with established humanitarian coordination platforms. These include local coordination structures linked to the Child Protection Area of Responsibility under the Global Protection Cluster, as well as Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) Technical Working Groups. Additionally, adherence to the Minimum Standards for Child Protection in Humanitarian Action, particularly standards 10 and 16, and the technical guidance provided in the Inter-Agency Standing Committee Guidelines on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in Emergency Settings, as well as the MHPSS Minimum Services Package, is essential. The evidence supporting the effectiveness of parenting interventions in humanitarian settings primarily pertains to selective prevention interventions targeting parents and caregivers identified as being at elevated risk of maltreatment. Indicated interventions, which are similar in content to universal and selective interventions, often include additional components such as trauma care. These interventions typically require a higher level of professional skill and training compared to universal or selective approaches. Group-based delivery of interventions has been found to be beneficial for sharing problems and solutions, while individualized interventions allow for closer relationships and tailored support from providers. Rapidly scaling parenting interventions in emergency settings may not always be feasible, particularly when addressing the needs of parents recently affected by crises. Research priorities in this area include studying the effectiveness of parenting interventions in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) for preventing child maltreatment, as well as examining outcomes such as child behavioral and emotional problems, parental mental health, and parenting stress. More studies are needed to include self-reported child outcomes related to maltreatment experiences, provided it is safe and developmentally appropriate to do so. Most existing studies have been conducted in conflict zones, with limited research on natural disasters or climate-related crises such as crop failures, droughts, floods, or typhoons. Given the increasing frequency of humanitarian crises due to climate change, future research in these settings is recommended. Additionally, research on the cost-effectiveness of parenting interventions and implementation issues, such as program length, cost, integration with other social and economic support systems, and training of lay community members, is needed. Clear specification of populations, delivery mechanisms, and settings, as well as addressing risks of bias, is critical when conducting such research. Parenting interventions for children aged 0–3 years are particularly important, as this age group is highly vulnerable to maltreatment and harsh parenting. These interventions teach nurturing, nonviolent parenting skills, which can positively influence parenting behaviors for older children. Strengthening responsive caregiving and early learning opportunities through play and communication activities enhances caregiver sensitivity and responsiveness to children’s needs and promotes positive caregiver-child interactions. These interventions are effective in improving positive parenting practices, such as praise, warmth, and appropriate discipline, as well as parental mental health. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines emphasize the importance of responsive caregiving and early learning activities for all infants and children during their first three years of life. Parents and caregivers should be supported to provide these essential elements of care. Psychosocial interventions to support maternal mental health should also be integrated into early childhood health and development services. While the WHO Early Childhood Development (ECD) guidelines do not specifically focus on child maltreatment, the recommended interventions are likely to reduce risk factors for maltreatment and harsh parenting. Evidence from global systematic reviews indicates that parenting interventions for children aged 0–3 years are effective in improving cognitive, language, socioemotional, and motor development. These interventions are particularly impactful in LMICs, where stronger effects have been observed compared to high-income countries. Updated searches for the present guidelines identified additional randomized controlled trials in LMICs, with some reporting beneficial effects on harsh parenting and maltreatment outcomes. In summary, parenting interventions are a critical component of efforts to prevent child maltreatment and enhance parent-child relationships, particularly in humanitarian settings. Continued research and adaptation of these interventions to specific contexts and populations are essential to maximize their effectiveness and reach.
